title: Billy Lustig, Tommy Dorsey and the Little Club pay
summary: He negotiated pay for the Little Club job, then went to Chicago with Billy Lustig where he practiced with Tommy Dorsey, who also played fine trumpet.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Yeah, it was on Common and Drive. Tony DiNopolis had a place there. So they had a band from Scranton, Pennsylvania. Yeah, another one you're talking about. Yeah, sure. So Billy Lustig. So he came to the Palace and he says, Joe, Tony DiNopolis told him to come here and ask you if you want to take this job after you get off the theater. I said, yeah, how much you pay? He said, well I'll give you $100 and a quarter. I said, what? $100 and a quarter? I said, the trombone player had to go home and get operated. I said, I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take what you give the other trombone player. He said, well I can't give you that. I said, well forget about it. So he said, well I'm sorry. I said, well I'm sorry. I said, okay, that's all right. So we went back and Tony DiNopolis says, did you hire Santa? He says, he wants too much money. He said, well how much do you want to pay him? He said, well how much do you want to pay him? He said, well how much do you want to pay him? the doctor says, did you hire a Santa? He says, he wants too much money. He said, well how much you want to pay him? He said, I want to, he said, well how much you gave the other trombone player? He said, well give him the same, give him the same thing, see. So he came back and he said, well good job, I got $200. And I was making $75 at the Powell Street, the scale was $45, I was making $75. And you know when I said 19, 20, 21, 22. That's a lot of money. No tax. So then I went to Chicago with Billy Lustig and I couldn't get there. I had to give two weeks notice for Keir to see before I could get to Chicago. So he used Tommy Darcy on the trombone. So I got there, Tommy Darcy played and I played. And he used to say, Barney says, you get a big tone on the trombone. I said, yes, but you get a pretty tone on it. He said, yeah, but my tone ain't bigger than yours, you know, one of those things. So I used to love to hear him play because he played so beautiful. Then the trumpet player, you heard of Johnny Bystorfer?

Yeah, you knew him. All right. Johnny Bystorfer got sick for about three weeks. So Tommy takes the trumpet and plays the big show. I can believe it. A beautiful trumpet. Oh man. I said, how in the hell can you play trumpet and take the trumpet? He used to like the trombones. He wanted to play trombone. But he used to play that show, cut that show like that.
He sounded like Joe Olive on trumpet to me. Some of the records. He sounded like Joe Olive on trumpet. No. Somebody could play Rattie on trumpet.

No, he sounded like Harry James or Spivak or something like that. Oh, he had a beautiful tone. Everything, numb pressure and all that. Tommy played beautiful. Look at it. But he had to get on that trombone. But him and I, and he used to practice in the hotel room. Gee, nine o'clock in the morning. We'd go home about four o'clock in the morning. Get up at nine o'clock and practice with records and all that stuff. We got to be pretty good friends. Well, you know who bought Jack Teagarden first trombone? Me. You did? Jack Teagarden was working at, what's up? I'm not Lake Charles, St. Charles, Louisiana. What's that little town? Lake Charles. No, not Lake Charles. It's close by here.
